Objective
Learn to add polynomials by matching terms with identical variable powers. You will combine coefficients and keep each exponent unchanged.
Like terms
Three x squared and five x squared are like terms, but three x squared and five x are not. Compare the variable part before adding.
Core rule
Add the coefficients of like terms and copy the common variable power. For example, two x cubed plus four x cubed equals six x cubed.
Linear example
Add three x plus four to two x minus seven. The variable terms give five x and the constants give negative three, so the answer is five x minus three.
Quadratic example
Add three x squared minus two x plus five to x squared plus seven x minus nine. The sum is four x squared plus five x minus four.
Missing powers
If a polynomial has no x squared term, treat its coefficient as zero. This helps align different powers without accidentally dropping a term.
Negative signs
When adding negative coefficients, keep their signs. Six m squared plus negative two m squared is four m squared, not eight m squared.
Fractions
One half x squared plus one third x squared is five sixths x squared. Use a common denominator before adding fractional coefficients.
Context
Adding two trail lengths means adding their polynomial expressions. Keep the same units and combine the quadratic, linear, and constant terms.
Multivariable terms
Two a to the fourth b and negative seven a to the fourth b combine to negative five a to the fourth b. Other exponent patterns remain separate.
Exam strategy
Group terms by exponent, add signed coefficients, and write the result in descending powers. Substitute a test value to check the identity.
Recap
Polynomial addition never adds exponents. Match like terms, add coefficients, preserve unmatched terms, and practice the eighteen questions before the test.
